guide.summary: Unit 2, the most heavily weighted, compares executives, legislatures, and judiciaries across the six course countries: parliamentary, presidential, and semi-presidential systems; heads of state and government; term limits; legislative structure and power; judicial independence and review; and how institutions check or fail to check power.

sections.heading: Executive systems
sections.body: In a parliamentary system (UK), the head of government (prime minister) comes from and depends on the confidence of the legislature; a vote of no confidence can bring down the government; the head of state (the monarch) is ceremonial. In a presidential system (Mexico, Nigeria), a directly elected president is both head of state and government, with a fixed term and separation of powers. In a semi-presidential system (Russia), a powerful elected president coexists with a prime minister who manages government and needs legislative approval. Term limits: Mexico's president serves one six-year term (sexenio) with no reelection; Nigeria's president serves up to two four-year terms; Russia's president serves six-year terms, and 2020 constitutional amendments reset Putin's term count. Iran's Supreme Leader (head of state, chosen by the Assembly of Experts) outranks the elected president. In China, the CCP General Secretary holds real power, also serving as state president and military commission chair; presidential term limits were removed in 2018; the premier heads the State Council.

sections.heading: Legislatures
sections.body: UK: bicameral Parliament; the elected House of Commons is dominant; the appointed/hereditary House of Lords can delay but not block most legislation. Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament's acts are supreme. Mexico: bicameral Congress (Chamber of Deputies and Senate) that has become more assertive since the end of PRI dominance. Russia: bicameral Federal Assembly; the State Duma is elected, and the Federation Council represents regions; both rarely challenge the president. Iran: unicameral Majles (Islamic Consultative Assembly), whose laws must be approved by the Guardian Council for conformity with Islam and the constitution; the Expediency Council resolves disputes. China: the unicameral National People's Congress (about 3,000 delegates) formally holds supreme power but largely approves party decisions; its Standing Committee acts between sessions. Nigeria: bicameral National Assembly (Senate and House of Representatives).

sections.heading: Judiciaries
sections.body: An independent judiciary with judicial review can check other branches. The UK Supreme Court (established 2009) can rule on legality but can't overturn acts of Parliament (it can issue declarations of incompatibility with human-rights law). Mexico's Supreme Court has judicial review; a 2024 reform introduced popular election of judges, raising debates about independence. Nigeria's Supreme Court has judicial review and has ruled on election disputes. Russia's Constitutional Court has judicial review in theory but rarely challenges the president. Iran's judiciary is headed by an official appointed by the Supreme Leader and applies Islamic law. China's courts operate under party leadership and lack independence.

keyTakeaways: Parliamentary: PM depends on legislature (UK). Presidential: fixed term, separation (Mexico, Nigeria). Semi-presidential: Russia.
Mexico: one six-year term; Nigeria: two four-year terms.
Iran: Supreme Leader > president; Guardian Council vets laws and candidates.
China: party leadership controls state institutions; term limits removed 2018.
UK: parliamentary sovereignty; no judicial review over acts of Parliament.
Judicial independence is strongest in UK, Mexico, Nigeria; weak in Russia, Iran, China.
commonMistakes: Saying the UK monarch makes policy.
Thinking the House of Lords can permanently veto legislation.
Confusing the Guardian Council with the Assembly of Experts.
Calling China's NPC an independent legislature.
Assuming Russia's prime minister is the most powerful official.
examTips: Use institutional names precisely: Duma, Majles, NPC, House of Commons.
Explain how institutions check (or don't check) executives in each country.
Compare term limits and their changes (Russia 2020, China 2018).
Distinguish formal powers from actual practice.

practice.prompt:
Develop an argument that explains whether presidential or parliamentary systems are more effective in holding executives accountable.

Use one or more of the following course concepts in your response: separation of powers, vote of no confidence, term limits, judicial independence.

In your response, do the following:
- Respond with a thesis that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Support your claim with at least TWO pieces of specific and relevant evidence from one or more course countries.
- Use reasoning to explain why your evidence supports your claim.
- Respond to an opposing or alternative perspective using refutation, concession, or rebuttal.

rubric.description: Defensible claim with a line of reasoning.

1: one piece of specific, relevant evidence. 2: two pieces from course countries supporting the claim (e.g., UK votes of no confidence and PM resignations; Mexico's single-term limit; Nigeria's courts and 2015 turnover).
Explains how the evidence supports the thesis.
Responds to an opposing perspective with refutation, concession, or rebuttal.

practice.sampleResponse:
Parliamentary systems are more effective in holding executives accountable because the executive must keep the continuous confidence of the legislature and can be removed quickly without waiting for an election.

In the United Kingdom, the prime minister depends on the support of a majority in the House of Commons. If that support erodes, the governing party can replace its leader or the Commons can pass a vote of no confidence. British prime ministers have been forced from office mid-term when they lost the confidence of their own party, showing that accountability is ongoing rather than limited to election day.

By contrast, presidents with fixed terms can be difficult to remove. In Russia's semi-presidential system, the president dominates; the Duma rarely challenges him, and 2020 constitutional amendments reset presidential term limits, allowing Putin to remain in office far longer. Fixed terms and weak legislative checks let executives escape accountability.

Some argue presidential systems hold executives accountable through separation of powers and term limits, as in Mexico, where the president serves a single six-year term. It's true that Mexico's no-reelection rule prevents any president from entrenching himself. However, term limits only guarantee accountability at fixed intervals; during the term, removal requires impeachment, which is rare. A parliamentary executive faces constant scrutiny and can be replaced as soon as it loses support, making accountability more continuous and effective.
